label: Jensen, Markov, Chebyshev and Cauchy–Schwarz — mastery test (unseen)

items.stem: For a convex function g, Jensen's inequality states:
items.explanation: Convexity means the curve lies above each of its tangents, and taking expectations about the tangent at E(X) gives the result. For a CONCAVE g it reverses to ≤. Equality holds only when g is linear on the support of X.

items.stem: For a positive random variable X, E(1/X) compared with 1/E(X) is:
items.explanation: 1/x has second derivative 2/x³ > 0 on the positive half-line, so it is CONVEX and Jensen gives E(1/X) ≥ 1/E(X). Concretely, X taking 1 or 3 with probability ½ gives E(1/X) = 2/3 ≈ 0.667 against 1/E(X) = 0.5. Getting this direction wrong is the standard error in the topic.

items.stem: For a non-negative random variable X with distribution function F, ∫₀^∞ [1 − F(x)]dx equals:
items.explanation: The integral of the survival function is the mean. It follows from swapping the order of integration in E(X) = ∫₀^∞(∫₀^x dy)f(x)dx. Verified by quadrature: 1.000000 for Exponential(1), 0.500000 for Exponential(2) and 1.500000 for Uniform(0,3), matching the means exactly.
items.check: For Exponential(1), ∫₀^∞ e^(−x)dx = 1, which is indeed E(X).

items.stem: For a non-negative X, ∫₀^∞ 2x[1 − F(x)]dx equals:
items.explanation: The general identity is E(Xⁿ) = ∫₀^∞ n x^(n−1)[1 − F(x)]dx, and n = 2 produces the 2x factor. Verified by quadrature as 2.000000, 0.500000 and 3.000000 for Exponential(1), Exponential(2) and Uniform(0,3), matching E(X²) in each case.
items.check: For Exponential(1), ∫₀^∞ 2x e^(−x)dx = 2Γ(2) = 2, which is E(X²).

items.stem: Markov's inequality states that for X ≥ 0 and a > 0:
items.explanation: Non-negativity is essential — without it the statement is false. It is proved from X ≥ a·1{X ≥ a} by taking expectations. Option D is closer to Chebyshev, which uses a variance rather than a mean.
items.check: It is tight for X = a with probability p and 0 otherwise, where E(X) = pa and P(X ≥ a) = p exactly.

items.stem: Chebyshev's inequality bounds P(|X − μ| ≥ 2σ) by:
items.explanation: The bound is 1/k² with k = 2, so 0.25. For a standard normal the true probability is only 0.045500 — the bound overstates it by a factor of 5.5 — but Chebyshev holds for every distribution with a finite variance, which is why it must accommodate the worst case.
items.check: At k = 1 the bound would be 1, which is no information at all, since every probability is at most 1.

items.stem: E(log X) ≤ log E(X) holds because log is:
items.explanation: log x has second derivative −1/x² < 0, so it is concave and Jensen reverses. Being increasing is true but irrelevant — the direction of Jensen depends only on curvature. Note this statement and E(1/X) ≤ 1/E(X) have identical form, yet one is true and the other false, precisely because 1/x is convex.

items.stem: Var(X) ≥ 0 is a special case of Jensen's inequality applied to:
items.explanation: g(x) = x² is convex, so E(X²) ≥ (E(X))², and rearranging gives E(X²) − (E X)² = Var(X) ≥ 0. The other three functions are either concave or give different consequences — 1/x gives E(1/X) ≥ 1/E(X), and log x and √x both point the other way.

items.stem: The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality applied to random variables yields:
items.explanation: Applying |E(XY)| ≤ √(E(X²)E(Y²)) to the centred variables gives Cov(X,Y)² ≤ Var(X)Var(Y), which rearranges to |ρ| ≤ 1. So the familiar bound on a correlation coefficient is this inequality, and its equality condition — linear dependence — is what makes |ρ| = 1 mean a perfect linear relationship.

items.stem: For a non-negative integer-valued X, E(X) equals:
items.explanation: The discrete analogue of the tail integral. Option B adds P(X ≥ 0) = 1, overstating by exactly 1; option A sums to 1, not to the mean. Verified for the geometric counting trials, where Σ(1−p)^(k−1) = 1/p gives 3.333333 at p = 0.3 and 2.000000 at p = 0.5.
items.check: For Geometric(0.25) the sum is 1/0.25 = 4, which matches the known mean 1/p.

items.stem: A non-negative random variable has mean 6. Markov's bound on P(X ≥ 30) is:
items.explanation: E(X)/a = 6/30 = 0.2. The bound uses nothing but the mean and non-negativity, and is usually very loose: for an exponential with mean 6 the true probability is e^(−5) = 0.006738, thirty times smaller.
items.check: Any probability bound must lie in [0, 1], which rules out option C immediately.

items.stem: Consider the four inequalities.
items.explanation: A is true — 1/x is convex. B is true: Chebyshev is Markov applied to (X − μ)². C is true, and it is why the bound cannot be improved. D is false — Markov requires non-negativity.
statements: E(1/X) ≥ 1/E(X) for a positive random variable.
There is a distribution attaining Chebyshev's bound exactly.
Markov's inequality holds for any variable with a finite mean.

A.why: True. 1/x has second derivative 2/x³ > 0 on x > 0, so it is convex and Jensen points that way. On Uniform(1,3) the two sides are 0.549306 and 0.5.

B.why: True — apply Markov to the non-negative variable (X − μ)² at the level k²σ². The squaring is what turns 1/a into 1/k², and it is also why a variance rather than a mean is required.

C.why: True: mass 1/(2k²) at each of μ ± kσ with the rest at μ. Verified at k = 2 and 3, where the variance comes to exactly 1.000000 and the tail probability exactly 1/k². So no smaller bound could be true for every distribution with a finite variance.

D.why: False — it requires X ≥ 0. The proof uses X ≥ a·1{X ≥ a}, which fails if X can be negative, and the conclusion is then simply untrue.

items.stem: X has mean 100 and standard deviation 10. Chebyshev's bound on P(|X − 100| ≥ 25) is:
items.explanation: The deviation is 25/10 = 2.5 standard deviations, so k = 2.5 and the bound is 1/6.25 = 0.16. Option A would be the bound at k = 2, which is the error of not dividing by σ.
items.check: For a normal the true probability at k = 2.5 is 0.012419, so the bound is about thirteen times too large — but it needs no distributional assumption.

items.stem: For k ≥ 1, which distribution attains Chebyshev's bound?
options: mass 1/(2k²) at each of μ ± kσ, the remainder at μ
none — the bound is never attained
items.explanation: For k ≥ 1, put mass 1/(2k²) at each of μ ± kσ and the remaining mass 1 − 1/k² at μ. The remaining mass is non-negative precisely when k ≥ 1. Its variance is 2 × (1/(2k²)) × (kσ)² = σ², and P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) = 1/k² exactly, so it attains Chebyshev's bound. For 0 < k < 1 the bound exceeds 1 and is vacuous; this three-point construction would require a negative central mass.

items.stem: Why is Chebyshev's inequality so loose for a normal distribution?
options: the normal has no finite variance
it is distribution-free, so its value is set by the worst case rather than by the normal
it applies only to discrete distributions
the inequality is incorrectly stated in most textbooks
items.explanation: The bound must hold for every distribution with a finite variance, including the three-point one that attains it, so it cannot be tighter. For a normal the ratio of truth to bound falls from 0.317 at k = 1 to 0.182 at k = 2 and 0.024 at k = 3 — the slack grows, because the bound decays as 1/k² while a normal tail decays like e^(−k²/2).

items.stem: Var(X) = 9 and Var(Y) = 16. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds |Cov(X,Y)| by:
items.explanation: Cov² ≤ Var(X)Var(Y) = 144, so |Cov| ≤ 12. Equality holds only when Y is a linear function of X, and dividing through gives |ρ| = |Cov|/12 ≤ 1 — the familiar statement.
items.check: Option C is the product of the variances, which bounds the SQUARE of the covariance, not the covariance itself.

items.stem: Consider finer points about these bounds.
items.explanation: A is true — the density is positive at 0 and the integral diverges. B is true: Cantelli gives 1/(1+k²) = 0.2 at k = 2. C is true, and it shows Markov's weakness lay in the choice of function. D is false — at k = 1 the bound is 1, which is vacuous.
statements: E(1/X) is infinite for an Exponential(1) variable.
For a one-sided tail, Cantelli's bound 1/(1 + k²) improves on Chebyshev.
Markov applied to e^(tX) gives an exponentially small bound.
Chebyshev's inequality is informative at k = 1.

A.why: True. The density of Exponential(1) is 1 at the origin, so ∫(1/x)e^(−x)dx diverges there. Jensen still holds with an infinite left side, but a simulation drifts upward with n — roughly 15 at a million draws and 40 at ten million.

B.why: True: at k = 2 Cantelli gives 0.2 against the 0.25 that halving the two-sided bound would suggest. The improvement comes from using the one-sidedness, so a two-sided bound should never simply be halved.

C.why: True — that is the Chernoff bound, P(X ≥ a) ≤ E(e^(tX))/e^(ta) optimised over t. It shows the looseness of Markov came from applying it to X rather than to a rapidly growing function of X.

D.why: False. At k = 1 the bound is 1/1 = 1, and since every probability is at most 1 the inequality says nothing whatever. It becomes informative only beyond one standard deviation.

items.stem: Let X be non-negative with distribution function F. Which set of statements is correct? A. ∫₀^∞ 2x[1 − F(x)]dx = E(X²). B. ∫₀^∞ [1 − F(x)]dx = E(X). C. E(1/X) ≤ 1/E(X). D. E(log X) ≤ log E(X).
items.explanation: A and B are the tail identities, both verified by quadrature on three distributions. D is true because log is concave. C is FALSE: 1/x is convex, so Jensen gives E(1/X) ≥ 1/E(X) — on Uniform(1,3) the two sides are 0.549306 and 0.5. This is the June 2026 question, and its difficulty is that C and D have identical written form and differ only in the curvature of the function.

items.stem: For X ~ Exponential(1), compare Markov's bound at a = 3 with the true probability.
options: bound 0.3333 against a truth of 0.0498, a factor of 6.7
items.explanation: The bound is E(X)/a = 1/3 = 0.333333 and the truth is e^(−3) = 0.049787. The gap widens further out: at a = 5 the bound is 0.2 against 0.006738, a factor of 30, because Markov's bound decays as 1/a while an exponential tail decays geometrically.
items.check: Markov's bound must always be at least the true probability, so the larger of the two numbers has to be the bound.

items.stem: Chebyshev's inequality is loose, yet it proves the weak law of large numbers. Why is the looseness not a problem there?
options: because the weak law does not require an inequality
because the sample mean is normally distributed
because the bound becomes tight as n grows
because the bound σ²/(nε²) tends to zero whatever the constant, so only the limit matters
items.explanation: Applied to X̄ₙ, Chebyshev gives P(|X̄ₙ − μ| ≥ ε) ≤ σ²/(nε²), and a loose constant multiplying 1/n still goes to zero. That is the clearest case of a slack bound being entirely adequate: the inequality is a tool for proving asymptotic statements, not for computing probabilities that could be computed exactly.
